p.src: It was a rather cold afternoon. Having grown tired of reading “The Words of a Fool,” I set out to visit the philosopher Magg. At a corner in a deserted-looking street, I found a kappa as thin as a mosquito leaning vacantly against a wall. And there was no mistaking it: this was the very kappa who had once stolen my fountain pen. Thinking I had him now, I stopped a burly policeman who happened to be passing by. “Please question that kappa over there. He stole my fountain pen about a month ago.” The policeman raised the club in his right hand—policemen in this country carry yew clubs instead of swords— and called out to the kappa, “Hey, you!” I wondered whether the kappa might make a run for it. But, contrary to my expectations, he calmly walked up to the policeman. What was more, he stood there with his arms folded, haughtily looking me and the policeman up and down. The policeman, however, did not lose his temper. He took a notebook from the pouch on his belly and immediately began his interrogation. “Your name?” “Gluck.” “Occupation?” “Until two or three days ago, I was a postman.” “Very well. Now, according to this gentleman’s statement, you stole his fountain pen.” “Yes, I stole it about a month ago.” “What for?” “I meant to give it to my child as a toy.” “And the child?” For the first time, the policeman fixed the kappa before him with a piercing stare. “The child died a week ago.” “Do you have the death certificate?” The thin kappa took a sheet of paper from the pouch on his belly. p.src: I stared at the policeman, utterly dumbfounded. Meanwhile, the thin kappa went off, muttering something under his breath and leaving us behind. At last I recovered my wits and asked the policeman: “Why aren’t you arresting that kappa?” “That kappa is innocent.” “But he stole my fountain pen—” “It was to make a toy for his child, wasn’t it? But that child is dead. If you have any doubts, look up Article 1285 of the Penal Code.” With that curt remark, the policeman strode briskly away somewhere. There was nothing I could do, so I hurried to Magg’s house, repeating “Article 1285 of the Penal Code” under my breath. Magg the philosopher was fond of entertaining guests. That very day, Judge Pep, Dr. Chak, Gael, the president of a glass company, and several others had gathered in his dim room, sending tobacco smoke curling up beneath a lantern of seven-colored glass. The presence of Judge Pep suited me perfectly. p.src: ‘No offender, whatever the crime committed, may be punished after the circumstances that caused the crime to be committed have ceased to exist.’ In your case, in other words, that kappa was once a parent, but is no longer one; consequently, the crime itself has naturally ceased to exist.”

u.src: ‘No offender, whatever the crime committed, may be punished after the circumstances that caused the crime to be committed have ceased to exist.’ In your case, in other words, that kappa was once a parent, but is no longer one; consequently, the crime itself has naturally ceased to exist.”

p.src: “That seems quite unreasonable.” “Don’t talk nonsense. It is precisely treating a kappa who was once a parent and one who is still a parent as identical that is unreasonable. Ah yes, under Japanese law they are treated as identical, aren’t they? We find that exceedingly comical. Heh-heh-heh-heh-heh-heh-heh-heh-heh-heh.” Pepp tossed away his cigarette and gave a listless little chuckle. The one who now joined the conversation was Chack, who had little connection with the law. Chack adjusted his pince-nez and asked me this question: “Is there capital punishment in Japan too?” “Of course there is. In Japan, the punishment is hanging.” I had begun to feel a certain antipathy toward Pepp for remaining so cool and composed, so I took this opportunity to direct a barb at him. “I suppose capital punishment in this country is administered more civilly than in Japan?” “Naturally, it is civilized.” Pepp remained perfectly calm. “In this country we use nothing like hanging. On rare occasions, we do use electricity. But usually we do not even use electricity. We merely tell the condemned kappa the name of his crime.” “Is that alone enough to kill a kappa?” “Indeed it is. Our nervous systems are more delicate than yours, you see.” “That is not confined to capital punishment. The same method is sometimes used for murder—” Gael, the company president, his whole face dyed purple by the light through the colored glass, gave us an affable smile. “Only recently, a socialist called me ‘You thief!’ and very nearly brought on a heart attack.” “It seems to happen surprisingly often. A lawyer I once knew actually died from the same cause.” I turned toward the kappa who had interjected—Magg the philosopher.

p.src: As always, Magg spoke with an ironic smile on his lips, without looking at anyone.

p.src: “Someone called that kappa a frog—and of course you know that in this country, to be called a frog is to be called an inhuman wretch. —Am I a frog? Or am I not a frog? He pondered those questions every day until at last he died.” “Then it was suicide, in other words.” “Although the fellow who called him a frog said it with the intention of killing him. From your point of view, I suppose even that would still be called suicide…” It was just as Magg said this. Suddenly, from beyond the wall of the room—from the poet Tock’s house, without a doubt—a single sharp pistol shot rang out, seeming to make the very air recoil.
